text: The psychological muscle you have to build to be a great leader is to be able to click in the abyss and go, 'Okay, that way's slightly better. We're going to go that way.
speaker: Ben Horowitz
context: Lenny asks Ben about the difficulty and pain of being a CEO and why so many people still want to start companies despite this reality. Ben explains that leaders must develop the psychological strength to make extremely difficult decisions where all options appear terrible. He emphasizes that true leadership value comes from making unpopular but necessary decisions that others wouldn't make on their own.
text_ko: 훌륭한 리더가 되려면 길러야 할 심리적 근육(psychological muscle)이 있어요. 그건 불확실한 심연에서 '클릭'하듯(click in the abyss) 결단을 내리고, "좋아요, 저쪽이 조금 더 나아 보이네요. 그쪽으로 갈게요"라고 말할 수 있는 능력이에요.
text_zh: 要成为优秀领导者，你得练就这样的心理素质：即使在最绝望的时候，也能瞬间调整状态，然后说"好，那个方向稍微好一点，我们就往那边走。"
text_es: El músculo psicológico que tienes que desarrollar para ser un gran líder es poder hacer clic en el abismo y decir: "Bueno, por ahí se ve un poco mejor. Vamos por ese camino."
key_sentence: the psychological muscle you have to build to be a great leader is to be able to click in the abyss
original_text: The psychological muscle you have to build to be a great leader is to be able to click in the abyss and go, 'Okay, that way's slightly better. We're going to go that way. If everybody agrees with the decision, then you didn't add any value because they would've done that without you.' So the only value you ever add is when you make a decision that most people don't like.

text: What I was trying to get out in Good Product Manager, Bad Product Manager, was the job is fundamentally a leadership job. And it's a tricky leadership job because nobody is actually reporting to you.
speaker: Ben Horowitz
context: Lenny mentions Ben's famous piece 'Good Product Manager, Bad Product Manager' and asks about its relevance today. Ben explains that when he wrote this internal document at Netscape, he was trying to help product managers understand that their role is primarily about leadership, not just completing tasks like writing specs or conducting interviews. The challenge is that PMs must lead without having direct authority over the people they need to influence.
text_ko: 제가 'Good Product Manager, Bad Product Manager'에서 말하려던 건, 프로덕트 매니저(Product Manager)라는 직무가 근본적으로 리더십 역할(leadership job)이라는 거예요. 그리고 이건 까다로운 리더십 역할인데, 그 이유는 실제로 아무도 당신에게 직접 보고하지 않기 때문이에요.
text_zh: 我在《好的产品经理，坏的产品经理》里想说的是，这个岗位本质上就是个领导职位。而且这个领导职位特别有挑战性，因为实际上没有人直接向你汇报。
text_es: Lo que trataba de transmitir en "Good Product Manager, Bad Product Manager" es que el trabajo es fundamentalmente un puesto de liderazgo. Y es un liderazgo complicado porque en realidad nadie te reporta directamente.
key_sentence: It's a tricky leadership job with no one reporting to you.

vocabulary.definition: In a basic or essential way; at the core or root of something.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, 'fundamentally' is often used to emphasize the essential nature of a concept, principle, or role, such as the core responsibilities of a manager.
vocabulary.nuance: This term suggests a deep-seated truth and is typically used to highlight the importance of foundational aspects in a discussion.

vocabulary.definition: The action of leading a group or organization, often involving the ability to influence and guide others toward achieving goals.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, effective leadership is crucial for motivating teams, driving strategic initiatives, and fostering a positive organizational culture.
vocabulary.nuance: While often associated with authority, leadership can also refer to informal influence and the ability to inspire others, regardless of one's official position.

vocabulary.definition: Difficult to deal with or accomplish; often involving complex or delicate situations.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a 'tricky' situation may refer to challenges in negotiations, project management, or interpersonal dynamics that require careful handling.
vocabulary.nuance: This term can imply a sense of caution or complexity, suggesting that a straightforward approach may not be effective.

vocabulary.definition: The act of providing information, often in the form of data or analysis, to stakeholders or management.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business environments, 'reporting' is essential for tracking performance, making informed decisions, and ensuring accountability within teams and projects.
vocabulary.nuance: This term can also imply a formal structure and regularity, as in scheduled reports, but can vary in context from informal updates to detailed analyses.

text: Probably one of my bigger ones on that was we went public with $2 million in trailing 12 months revenue at 18 months old. That's obviously a bad idea. But the truth of it was the alternative was going bankrupt, and that's a worse idea.
speaker: Ben Horowitz
context: Ben is discussing the importance of running towards fear and making difficult decisions as a leader, even when both available options seem terrible. He shares a personal example from his CEO experience where he had to choose between two bad alternatives. Ben explains that hesitation is the worst thing a leader can do, and sometimes you must choose the less terrible option even when it will result in harsh criticism.
text_ko: 그와 관련해 제가 저지른 큰 실수 중 하나는 설립한 지 18개월밖에 안 됐을 때 최근 12개월 매출(trailing 12 months revenue)이 200만 달러인 상태로 상장했다는 거예요. 분명히 그건 안 좋은 결정이었어요. 그런데 사실 다른 선택지는 파산하는 것뿐이었고, 그건 더 나쁜 선택이었어요.
text_zh: 我犯的比较大的错误之一就是，公司才18个月大的时候我们就上市了，当时过去12个月的收入才200万美元。这明显是个糟糕的决定。但实话说，当时要么这样，要么破产，破产显然更糟糕。
text_es: Probablemente uno de mis errores más grandes fue que salimos a bolsa con solo 2 millones de dólares en ingresos de los últimos 12 meses cuando la empresa tenía apenas 18 meses. Obviamente es una pésima idea. Pero la realidad era que la alternativa era quebrar, y eso es aún peor.
key_sentence: Trailing 12 months revenue at $2 million was a bad idea, worse than going bankrupt.

vocabulary.definition: Bankrupt refers to a legal status of a person or organization that cannot repay the debts it owes to creditors.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business world, declaring bankruptcy can lead to liquidation or reorganization, impacting stakeholders, employees, and the overall market perception of the company.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often implies a failure or inability to manage finances effectively, which can carry a stigma in professional settings.

text: The only reason to start a company is because you have an irrational desire to do so, because it's not worth the money.
speaker: Ben Horowitz
context: Lenny asks Ben who should not start companies and what advice he gives to people considering entrepreneurship who may not understand what they're getting into. Ben shares wisdom from John Reed, former CEO of Citigroup, about the true motivation needed for starting a company. He emphasizes that founders need a deeper purpose beyond financial gain to survive the inevitable challenges of building a company.
text_ko: 회사를 시작하는 유일한 이유는 돈 때문이 아니라, 돈으로 보상할 수 없을 만큼 도무지 떨쳐낼 수 없는 비합리적인 열망이 있기 때문이에요.
text_zh: 创业的唯一理由就是你有一种说不清道不明的冲动想去做这件事，因为单纯为了赚钱的话根本不值得。
text_es: La única razón para montar una empresa es porque tienes unas ganas irracionales de hacerlo, porque por dinero no vale la pena.
key_sentence: An irrational desire to start a company is essential to get you an outcome.
original_text: The only reason to start a company is because you have an irrational desire to do so, because it's not worth the money. So I think if you're doing it for the money, that's a very bad reason and it will be extremely difficult to get you an outcome.

vocabulary.definition: Not based on reason or logic; exhibiting a lack of sound judgment.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, an 'irrational' decision may refer to choices made based on emotions or impulses rather than data-driven analysis, often seen in startup founders who pursue their vision passionately.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'irrational' typically has a negative connotation, in entrepreneurial contexts, it can sometimes imply a boldness that drives innovation.

vocabulary.definition: The value or importance of something, often measured in terms of financial return or utility.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'worth' can refer to the valuation of a company, its assets, or the potential return on investment for stakeholders.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'worth' often relates to monetary value, it can also encompass non-financial aspects like brand reputation or social impact.

text: You don't make people great. You find people that make you great, that make the company great, that you learned from, not the other way around.
speaker: Ben Horowitz
context: Lenny shares a story from Ali Ghodsi (CEO of Databricks) about advice Ben gave him when he became CEO regarding low performers on his team. Ben explains the concept of 'managerial leverage' - the difference between spending time developing people versus finding people who can drive the company forward independently. He emphasizes that as a CEO, you should focus on hiring people who can teach you and push the company forward, rather than trying to coach people in areas where you lack expertise.
text_ko: 사람을 위대하게 만드는 건 당신이 하는 일이 아니에요. 중요한 건 당신을 위대하게 만들어 주는 사람들, 회사를 위대하게 만들어 주는 사람들, 그리고 당신이 배운 사람들을 찾아내는 거예요. 그 반대가 아니에요.
text_zh: 你不是去培养牛人，而是要找到那些能让你变得更厉害、让公司变得更强的人，是你从他们身上学东西，不是反过来。
text_es: No es que tú hagas grande a la gente. Lo que tienes que hacer es encontrar gente que te haga grande a ti, que haga grande a la empresa, gente de la que tú aprendas, no al revés.
key_sentence: You find people that make you great, that make the company great, that you learned from, not the other way around.
original_text: You don't make people great. You find people that make you great, that make the company great, that you learned from, not the other way around. What's leverage is if you're telling me what you should do and how you can push the company forward, that's leverage, then I'm getting more than I'd have if you weren't there.

vocabulary.definition: Of an exceptionally high quality, standard, or degree; often used to describe individuals, teams, or outcomes that exceed expectations.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, the term 'great' is frequently used to evaluate leadership qualities, company culture, or innovative products that set benchmarks in the industry.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'great' is a positive descriptor, it can be subjective and may require further context to clarify the specific attributes that contribute to greatness.

vocabulary.definition: Gained knowledge, skills, or insights through experience, observation, or instruction from others.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, 'learned from' emphasizes the importance of mentorship, collaboration, and continuous improvement through shared experiences and feedback.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase highlights the value of humility and openness to learning from others, which is essential for personal and organizational growth.

text: There's a very consistent thing that happens, which is when somebody doesn't make it and it kind of starts with confidence is the way I would put it. And then if you lose confidence, what happens is you hesitate on the next decision.
speaker: Ben Horowitz
context: Lenny asks Ben when it actually makes sense to replace a founder as CEO, flipping the question about A16Z's philosophy of helping founders stay in their roles. Ben explains the pattern he's observed when founders fail as CEOs. He describes how the natural mistakes that come with learning to run a company can lead to a loss of confidence, which then creates hesitation in decision-making, ultimately leading to organizational dysfunction.
text_ko: 항상 비슷한 일이 생겨요. 누군가 잘 안 되기 시작하면, 제 표현대로라면 그건 자신감에서부터 시작돼요. 자신감을 잃으면 다음 결정을 내릴 때 주저하게 돼요.
text_zh: 有个很常见的现象，就是当有人做不成事的时候，我觉得根源往往是自信心出了问题。一旦失去自信，接下来做决定的时候就会犹豫不决。
text_es: Hay algo que pasa de manera muy consistente, y es cuando alguien no la logra, y yo diría que todo empieza con el tema de la confianza. Y luego, si pierdes la confianza, lo que pasa es que dudas en la siguiente decisión.
key_sentence: Losing confidence means you hesitate on the next decision.

vocabulary.definition: Showing steady conformity to the same principles, course, or form; unchanging in nature over time.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, consistency is crucial for maintaining brand identity and ensuring reliable performance in products or services.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'consistent' often has a positive connotation, it can imply a lack of innovation if overemphasized.

vocabulary.definition: The feeling or belief that one can rely on someone or something; a firm trust in one's abilities or qualities.
vocabulary.businessContext: Confidence is essential in business negotiations and leadership, as it influences decision-making and team morale.
vocabulary.nuance: While confidence can inspire trust, overconfidence may lead to reckless decisions or misjudgments.

vocabulary.definition: To pause before taking action, often due to uncertainty or indecision.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, hesitation can lead to missed opportunities or delays in project timelines, particularly in fast-paced environments.
vocabulary.nuance: Hesitation can indicate caution, but excessive hesitation may be viewed negatively as a lack of decisiveness.

vocabulary.definition: A conclusion or resolution reached after consideration; the act of making a choice between alternatives.
vocabulary.businessContext: Effective decision-making is vital in business strategy, impacting everything from resource allocation to market positioning.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'decision' is a neutral term, the context can imply varying levels of importance or urgency.

text: I think the thing that's right about what Sam is saying is the landscape is early, really early. The technology is very immature. As amazingly as it works, there's a long way to go to improve it.
speaker: Ben Horowitz
context: Lenny asks Ben about the potential AI bubble, referencing Sam Altman's recent comments that 'we're in a big bubble.' Ben analyzes Sam's statement, first noting that it's strategically smart for Sam to say this as a CEO. He then gives his perspective on whether AI is actually in a bubble, explaining that while he doesn't think it's a financial bubble like the dot-com era, there could be competitive disruption due to the immaturity of the technology.
text_ko: 샘이 한 말 중에서 맞는 건 지금 시장(landscape)이 아직 아주 초기 단계라는 점이에요, 정말 초기예요. 기술(technology)도 굉장히 미성숙해요. 작동이 놀라울 만큼 잘 되긴 하지만, 개선해야 할 부분이 훨씬 많이 남아 있어요.
text_zh: 我觉得Sam说得对的地方是，整个行业还处在很早期的阶段，真的很早期。技术还很不成熟。虽然现在的效果已经很惊艳了，但要真正完善起来还有很长的路要走。
text_es: Creo que en lo que Sam tiene razón es que estamos en pañales, súper en pañales. La tecnología está muy verde todavía. Por más increíble que funcione, queda muchísimo camino por recorrer para mejorarla.
key_sentence: the landscape is early, really early.
original_text: I think the thing that's right about what Sam is saying is the landscape is early, really early. The technology is very immature. As amazingly as it works, there's a long way to go to improve it. So it's very possible when you have that much technological change, that the positions that these companies have achieved with their high revenue isn't sustainable.

vocabulary.definition: The overall view or environment in which a particular situation exists, often referring to the market or industry dynamics.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, 'landscape' often describes the competitive environment, including key players, trends, and opportunities within a specific sector.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'landscape' can refer to a broad overview, it is often used to imply a dynamic and evolving context that requires ongoing analysis.

vocabulary.definition: Not fully developed or lacking in sophistication; often used to describe technology or products that are in early stages of development.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech industry, 'immature' can refer to technologies or products that have not yet reached a level of reliability or functionality expected by users or investors.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'immature' can have a negative connotation, it may also indicate potential for growth and improvement in the future.
